analysis.one_liner: Creates privately owned, freely sellable water rights and lets private companies build water projects with eminent domain.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by three Republican House members, was sent to a House committee and its water subcommittee in 1991 and never received a vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The Abundant Water Act would have converted water rights in eleven Western states — and groundwater nationwide — into transferable private property recorded by the Interior Department, free to be sold like any asset. It would have stripped the Bureau of Reclamation of its power to veto transfers of water out of federally funded irrigation projects, preempted any state water law that conflicted with the scheme, and allowed private businesses to build and run water projects as public utilities, including with the power to condemn land.
analysis.who_benefits: Existing water users — especially large farms in the West, including those using water from taxpayer-subsidized federal reclamation projects — would receive perpetual certificates for the water they already use, based on their historical consumption, and could sell those certificates without losing them through nonuse. Prospective private water companies could apply to build and operate water projects with federal eminent domain power and fee revenue. Conservation buyers could purchase instream flow rights to keep water in rivers. The bill's stated public benefit is that making water sellable would push farmers to conserve, freeing water for cities and the environment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Western water holders and private water developers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a book-entry system of 'water certificates' that makes water rights private property that can be sold, exchanged, or inherited, and cannot be forfeited for nonuse.
Removes the Secretary of the Interior's authority to disapprove transfers of water rights away from any federal reclamation project, opening up water now locked into subsidized irrigation districts.

Requires each state to recognize instream flow rights for aesthetic, environmental, navigational, or recreational purposes, which would let conservation groups buy and hold water for rivers and wildlife.
Allows holders of two-thirds of an aquifer's groundwater certificates to pool and manage the aquifer jointly.

Lets private businesses apply for authority to construct and operate water projects as public utilities, charging user fees under Interior Department review, with condemnation authority 'as if the operator were a Federal entity.'

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would bear the cost of seeing water developed at public expense through federal reclamation projects converted into salable private assets for current users. States would lose control over their water allocation systems to federal preemption. Other water users and rural communities would depend on limited 'reasonable restrictions under State law' for protection against transfers that impair their supply — protections under state law that the same act overrides where inconsistent.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, states, and non-transferring water users

drawbacks.text: The act supersedes and preempts any inconsistent state law, stripping the eleven covered Western states of their traditional authority over water allocation, which is how those states currently protect neighbors, communities, and the public when water moves.

Initial certificates would be issued based on historical use — including average groundwater pumped between 1986 and 1990 — meaning the largest existing users, including farms using subsidized reclamation water, would receive the largest perpetual private claims.

Once issued, a water certificate could not be lost for failure to put the water to beneficial use, eliminating the 'use it or lose it' rule that Western states use as their main lever to move unused water to new needs.

Third-party protection against impaired water rights is left to 'reasonable restrictions under State law' even as the act preempts state laws inconsistent with its free-transfer scheme, leaving non-consenting users' safeguards uncertain.

Private operators would gain federal-style eminent domain power to condemn land for water projects, and while the Secretary reviews fees, the operator is guaranteed a 'reasonable rate of return' from public water infrastructure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core market idea has genuine upside even critics of farm water subsidies acknowledge: if water could move from low-value, heavily subsidized agriculture to cities and instream environmental uses, more people would get more value from the same drops. But the bill's design starts by handing current users — including recipients of subsidized federal water — perpetual, non-forfeitable certificates in water the public helped develop, then overrides the state systems that manage conflicts in the arid West. The public benefits were speculative and dependent on the Secretary's implementation; the windfall to existing large water users and the loss of state control were immediate and certain. As drafted, the costs outweighed the promised gains for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 1991, sent to the House Interior Committee and then its water subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. William Dannemeyer of California introduced the bill on June 19, 1991, joined by Reps. Philip Crane and Dana Rohrabacher.
The House referred it to the Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs the same day.
On July 1, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water, Power and Offshore Energy Resources — the last recorded action.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything concrete; the existing system held, which is what state water administrators and the irrigation and municipal users who operate under it preferred. Large existing water users also avoided the uncertainty of having their rights re-certified and put on a trading market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing water users and state water systems

for.name: Rep. William E. Dannemeyer
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the Abundant Water Act and introduced it in the House.

for.name: Reps. Philip Crane and Dana Rohrabacher
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction as its only cosponsors.

against.name: George Miller
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill; the committee never scheduled a markup or reported it out.

against.name: House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on June 19, 1991, and its water subcommittee held it; no further action was ever taken.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were Republicans and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted, but with only three cosponsors and no votes ever taken, the bill never drew a measurable party-line record.

industries.industry: Western irrigated agriculture, including federal reclamation project water users
industries.note: The bill would hand these users perpetual, non-forfeitable certificates in the water they already use — including water developed with taxpayer subsidies — and let them sell it to the highest bidder. Their gain is a public asset converted to private salable property, though the bill argues cities and the environment would benefit from what farms gave up.

industries.industry: Private water development and engineering companies
industries.note: Title II would let private businesses build and operate water projects as public utilities, with federal-style eminent domain and fee revenue subject to Interior rate review. A new avenue into what is now a government-run field.

industries.industry: State water administration in the eleven covered Western states
industries.note: Federal preemption would override state water allocation and transfer rules wherever they conflict with the act, shifting control over a core state resource to federal certificates and the Interior Department.

industries.industry: Municipal water suppliers and growing Western cities
industries.note: A functioning transfer market could move water from farms to urban users; the bill's findings argue that even small farm-efficiency gains would substantially increase water available to everyone else.
The bill would let them buy enforceable instream flow rights to keep water in rivers, but they would have to outbid consumptive users in the new market to do it.
